true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
queued timestamp is evaluated once at class definition

AssignmentSource declares `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`, which Python evaluates once when the class is defined rather than for each instance. Every AssignmentSource created after process start will therefore carry the import/startup time instead of its actual creation time. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each assignment source gets a fresh timestamp.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a datetime into Celery task kwargs

sync_group_assignee_outbound passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` directly as an apply_async kwarg, and to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict(), so `queued` remains a datetime object. Sentry/Celery task arguments must be serializable (JSON); enqueueing an inbound-triggered assignment can therefore fail to serialize, or in other transports round-trip queued as a string that AssignmentSource.from_dict() never parses back to datetime. Serialize queued with isoformat() in to_dict() and parse it in from_dict() to make the round-trip safe.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

Task unconditionally passes new assignment_source kwarg to all installations

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Occurrence tests do not verify the evaluated value passed to the hook

build_mock_occurrence_and_event ignores its value argument when constructing the IssueOccurrence and event_data, so tests cannot detect evaluate_group_key_value passing the wrong value to build_occurrence_and_event_data. This is visible here: group_2 has packet value 10 but the expected occurrence is built with value 6, and the assertion still passes. A regression passing e.g. the dedupe value or another group's value would go uncaught.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-joined shard metric tag corrupts multi-shard tags

When one process handles multiple shards, shard_tag is built as a comma-joined string such as '0,2' and emitted as a single metrics tag value (also for segment_size_bytes and wait_produce). Comma is the separator between tags in StatsD/DogStatsD-style encoding, so the backend can parse this as an extra valueless tag instead of one shard tag, breaking per-shard filtering and creating malformed tag sets. The wait_produce metric also inconsistently uses the key 'shards' while the others use 'shard'. Metrics should be emitted per shard or use a separator that is valid in a single tag value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid flusher process counts are silently accepted

SpanFlusher does not validate max_processes. An explicit 0 is converted by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` into one process per shard, silently ignoring the configured limit and potentially spawning far more processes than intended. A negative value produces `num_processes <= 0`, an empty process-to-shards map, and therefore no flusher processes at all; submit() then finds no unhealthy processes to report while spans continue to be committed after being written to Redis but are never flushed. The CLI option in sentry.consumers accepts any integer, so this invalid configuration is reachable via --flusher-processes.

New multi-flusher test never verifies flushing or the spawn path

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts process counts and shard-map totals, then joins; it never submits a span and never asserts that a process shared by multiple shards actually flushes a segment for each of its shards. All consumer tests also pass produce_to_pipe, which forces SpanFlusher into its threading.Thread branch, so the production spawn branch (run_with_initialized_sentry, pickling the per-shard SpansBuffer, and the new shards argument to SpanFlusher.main) is not exercised at all. A regression that breaks spawned flushers or drops all but one shard in a shared process would pass the new tests.

Restarted flusher is started without waiting for the old process to exit

When a process is unhealthy, _ensure_processes_alive() calls process.kill() but never join()s it before _create_process_for_shards() immediately starts a replacement for the same shards and overwrites self.processes[process_index]. kill() only signals termination, so the old and new flushers can briefly run concurrently against the same Redis shards, racing flush_segments()/done_flush_segments() and potentially producing the same segment twice to Kafka. The lost handle also prevents the caller from later confirming or reaping that specific child. The replacement should be started only after the killed process has been joined/reaped.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Closing a strategy permanently kills the shared queue pool that the factory reuses

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the queues and workers. That pool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() on every create_with_partitions() call (e.g. after a Kafka rebalance, when Arroyo closes the old strategy and creates a new one for the new assignment). Submits to the now-shutdown queues raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() catches at line 317 and then marks the offset complete, so messages for the new assignment can be committed without ever being processed. The factory only clears queue_pool in its own shutdown(), not when a strategy is closed.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() logs any exception from result_processor but unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() similarly marks offsets complete when decoding/grouping/enqueueing fails. The commit loop then treats those offsets as processed and commits them, contradicting the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee: transient processing failures or poison messages are silently dropped and will not be redelivered.

Kafka offsets are committed from a background thread instead of the Arroyo processor thread

_commit_loop runs on its own thread and invokes commit_function, which in result_consumer.py calls Arroyo's Commit callable. Arroyo strategies are expected to invoke commit from the strategy's submit/poll/close calls on the StreamProcessor thread; calling it concurrently from this thread races StreamProcessor's own offset/assignment handling and can commit offsets against a stale or revoked assignment. Additionally, each strategy instance created for a rebalance spawns another commit thread over the same shared OffsetTracker, so two threads can race get_committable_offsets()/mark_committed() and double-commit.

Offset scan is O(offset range) every second while a queue is blocked

get_committable_offsets() iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) for every partition on every 1-second commit loop iteration. The strategy's stated purpose is to survive a slow item blocking a queue; in exactly that case all later offsets accumulate in all_offsets/outstanding, so each poll rescans an ever-growing range (quadratic overall) and the sets grow without bound for as long as one offset is stuck, wasting CPU and memory.

OffsetTracker is never reset when partitions are revoked or reassigned

OffsetTracker keeps all_offsets, outstanding and last_committed forever, with no hook to clear a partition when Arroyo revokes it or when create_with_partitions is called with a new assignment. Stale outstanding offsets from a previous assignment block commits for a reassigned partition, and if offsets restart below the stale last_committed value (consumer-group reset, topic recreation, or reassignment with an earlier starting offset from the partitions mapping, which the strategy ignores), get_committable_offsets() can never advance past last_committed and commits silently stall.

Queues are unbounded, so the new strategy provides no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() always enqueues and returns successfully, never raising MessageRejected. Despite the class docstring claiming natural backpressure, Arroyo will keep consuming from Kafka while workers fall behind, accumulating messages and WorkItem/result objects in memory indefinitely when one queue is slow or stuck, risking OOM instead of pausing consumption.

close() stops the commit loop before draining queues, discarding commit progress

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown() to drain pending work. Workers then finish processing queued items and mark offsets complete, but no commit loop remains to commit those offsets and close() performs no final commit flush. On every graceful shutdown/rebalance, all work completed during the drain is therefore reprocessed on restart, causing duplicate result processing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every cache-hit-but-not-allowed Check now performs a full DB permission fetch

getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions no longer check permCache, so the getIdentityPermissions call at line 139 always runs the basic-role, team-membership and permission-store queries whenever the cached scope map does not allow the request, even when that scope map was just read fresh from permCache. The only mitigation is the per-(action,name,parent) denial entry, so checks against many distinct resource names (including legitimate UI probing or enumeration of non-existent UIDs) each trigger several DB queries; singleflight only deduplicates concurrent identical keys, not sequential requests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguously encoded and omits part of the request identity

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators and does not include identity type, group or resource. Grafana UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct tuples such as name='a_b', parent='c' and name='a', parent='b_c' produce the same key, and resources that map to the same action string can also share an entry. A denial cached for one resource can consequently fast-path-deny a different resource for 30s. Use an unambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or hashed components) and include the resource/group and identity type.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache blocks newly granted permissions and is never invalidated on allow

Check returns Allowed:false immediately when permDenialCache contains the key, before consulting fresh permissions or the DB, and the allowed paths (cached-allow at line 131 and DB-allow after line 146) never delete a denial entry. A denial recorded just before a dashboard/folder is created or a grant is added therefore keeps denying the creator/grantee for the full shortCacheTTL (30s), undermining the stated goal of letting creators access newly created resources. Concurrent requests make it worse: a request that started before a grant can finish afterwards, record a denial, and that denial then overrides another request's fresh allow result because nothing clears it.

Denied result from stale folder tree is promoted into a longer-lived denial

On a cached-permission miss Check re-queries only permissions from the DB; checkPermission still resolves folder inheritance through buildFolderTree, which serves the 30s-cached folder tree. For a dashboard/folder under a newly created folder, the inherited-permission check can therefore still fail after the DB re-query, and line 154 then stores that failure in permDenialCache for a fresh 30s. The stale-folder denial can thus persist up to roughly a folder-cache TTL plus a denial TTL, so the fix does not reliably let creators reach resources in newly created folders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered list is missing its React key

The 'grafana' case returns <GrafanaRuleListItem> without key={key}, unlike the datasource and unknown cases and unlike the previous GrafanaRuleLoader usage. Silence action does nothing for prom-only rules

The Silence menu item can now be shown via useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities and clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` where rule is the ruler rule. In the new list view rule is undefined, so SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer (which requires a rulerRule) never opens and silencing from the list silently fails.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete menu item is never shown in the prom-only list view

AlertRuleMenu now computes canDelete from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities so the list view (which no longer loads ruler rules) can authorize deletion, but the Delete item is still rendered only when `canDelete && rulerRule`. With rulerRule removed from the list view this condition is always false, so Pause/Unpause is unavailable there even when the new grafana prom ability grants it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty-expression filtering now happens before interpolation in shard splitting

The previous code interpolated all targets first (interpolateVariablesInQueries) and only then filtered out empty/hidden queries, so a target whose expr is a variable that expands to an empty string was dropped. The new code filters on the raw pre-interpolation expr (lines 50-52) and never re-checks after applyTemplateVariables, so a variable-backed expr that interpolates to '' is retained and flows into requestSupportsSharding/getSelectorForShardValues/fetchLabelValues and query execution as an empty LogQL query, instead of being ignored like empty queries elsewhere. Move the emptiness check (or add a second one) after interpolation in runShardSplitQuery.

Shard-split queries are interpolated twice

runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters), but each resulting sub-request is then passed to runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), which after this PR interpolates the same targets again with the same scopedVars/filters (querySplitting.ts:299). applyTemplateVariables is not an idempotent no-op: it performs template replacement and applies ad-hoc filters from request.filters, so a second pass can duplicate ad-hoc label/filter injection into an already-filtered LogQL expression (potentially producing duplicate matchers/filters or invalid LogQL) and can re-expand '$' sequences introduced by the first expansion (e.g. variable/label values containing '$'), corrupting the expression. The updated test even encodes this by expecting applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for one original target. Interpolate only once: either let shard splitting do the pre-shard interpolation and have runSplitQuery accept already-interpolated targets/skip re-interpolation, or remove the duplicate work while preserving the interpolation needed before fetchLabelValues/getSelectorForShardValues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin Request Completed log line loses traceID

Before this change logRequest explicitly added "traceID" from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) plus pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname to logParams. The new code replaces those params with m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only stores endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname via log.WithContextualAttributes -- it never stores a trace ID. Unless the infra logger independently injects trace IDs (grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext only adds stored contextual attributes), the 'Plugin Request Completed' line will no longer be correlatable by traceID, a regression for tracing/debugging plugin requests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards the receiving logger's recorded state

FromContext returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver or a logger sharing the receiver's Logs storage. LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that constructs a TestLogger, passes it to the middleware, and then asserts on that instance's InfoLogs.Calls/Message/Ctx will observe zero calls because the log was recorded on a throwaway instance. The fake should return f (or share its state) so FromContext logging remains observable in tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and FromContext logging are untested

This PR moves contextual-attribute enrichment out of MetricsMiddleware into the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware and makes LoggerMiddleware depend on it (and on middleware ordering in CreateMiddlewares) to retain endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname fields. No test is added for ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and no existing test verifies that a logger obtained via FromContext after this middleware emits those attributes or that LoggerMiddleware still emits them end-to-end. A middleware-ordering or context-key regression would therefore silently drop those fields without failing tests; the renamed metrics test even still declares TestInstrumentationMiddleware at metrics_middleware_test.go:21.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit enforcement has a count-then-insert race that admits devices beyond the limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices and then, in a separate DB session, inserts the new device if count < deviceLimit. There is no transaction, lock, or unique admission constraint tying the count to the insert, so two (or more) concurrent first-time requests on the same or different Grafana instances can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. Under a burst of new anonymous devices the limit is not reliably enforced.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected device is cached before the limit check, allowing it to bypass the limit on retry

tagDeviceUI inserts the device into localCache via SetDefault before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice then returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry remains, so the anonymous client's next request from the same device hits the cache at line 83, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate grants access even though the device was never admitted. The limit is therefore only enforced for the first attempt within the 29-minute cache TTL. The cache entry must only be set after a successful store, or deleted on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication is now synchronously blocked on device-store database calls

Authenticate previously tagged the device in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout context; it now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context. Every cache-miss anonymous request now waits on a COUNT query plus an INSERT/UPDATE (and, when at the limit, a second UPDATE) before an identity is returned, so slow or contended database calls directly add latency to, or stall until request cancellation, all anonymous page/API loads. Only ErrDeviceLimitReached needs to be decided synchronously; the previous decoupling for ordinary tagging latency has been removed.

Provider signature changed without updating Wire-generated dependency injection

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore and constructs the store itself via ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit) (line 43), and ProvideAnonDBStore itself now requires an int64. The checked-in Wire injector (pkg/server/wire_gen.go and the anonymous WireSet) is not updated in this PR, so it still passes an AnonStore to this constructor and cannot supply the new int64 argument to ProvideAnonDBStore; the server package will fail to compile / wire generation will fail until the injector is regenerated and updated.

updateDevice uses generic '?' placeholders unlike the Postgres-specific upsert path

CreateOrUpdateDevice carefully uses $1..$5 placeholders for Postgres in its INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement, but the new updateDevice (used for every request once the limit is reached) hardcodes '?' placeholders. On Postgres deployments this UPDATE will fail with a syntax/placeholder error instead of updating an already-admitted device, so existing anonymous devices are rejected with a database error as soon as the limit is reached, while SQLite/MySQL continue to work. The update statement needs dialect-specific placeholders like the insert path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists

Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579 use r.log.Error for routine, successful batch operations, including when err is nil and when no IDs were found. They also embed the entire ids slice, which can contain tens of thousands of IDs when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is large. In production this will flood error logs, trigger error-based alerting for non-errors, and create very large log lines every batch. These messages should be Debug (or Info at most), should not log a nil err as an error, and should log counts rather than full ID lists.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification

The cleanup service ticker is changed from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This is unrelated to splitting the annotation DELETE queries and makes all cleanup jobs, including the annotation scan/delete batches, run 10x more often. On large installations this increases database load and, because a cleanup run can take up to the 9-minute timeout while ticks are buffered, can cause back-to-back cleanup runs. Restore the 10-minute interval unless the change is intentional and justified.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteByIDs can exceed database bind-parameter limits for non-SQLite databases

deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with one placeholder per fetched ID, and only special-cases SQLite when the configured batch size exceeds 999. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable and unbounded here; on PostgreSQL/MySQL a large value (the new test itself uses 32767) can approach or exceed the driver's bind-parameter limit (e.g. 65535 on PostgreSQL), causing cleanup to fail every run, whereas the previous subquery DELETE had no host-parameter limit. Chunk deletes by len(ids) against a safe per-dialect limit instead of relying only on the SQLite/configured-batch-size check.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name in the metric kind label and DeleteCollection mislabels its legacy metric

On successful Delete, line 106 calls recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...) passing the object `name` where every other call site passes options.Kind as the kind label. This produces unbounded metric cardinality (one series per deleted object name) and breaks kind-based aggregation. Separately, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are never recorded and storage gets a spurious second sample. Fix line 106 to options.Kind and line 166 to recordLegacyDuration.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name in the metric kind label and DeleteCollection mislabels its legacy metric

On successful Delete, line 106 calls recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...) passing the object `name` where every other call site passes options.Kind as the kind label. This produces unbounded metric cardinality (one series per deleted object name) and breaks kind-based aggregation. Separately, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are never recorded and storage gets a spurious second sample. Fix line 106 to options.Kind and line 166 to recordLegacyDuration.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy Create races with the caller on the same object

Create passes the exact same `obj` to Storage.Create, then hands that same object to Legacy.Create in a background goroutine while returning `created` (which typically aliases obj) to the caller. The apiserver will read/serialize/mutate the returned object concurrently with the legacy store reading and mutating the same object (e.g. setting resource version, name, timestamps), which is a data race and can corrupt the response or the legacy write. The legacy goroutine must be given a DeepCopy of the object (ideally made before Storage.Create mutates it), not the shared pointer.

Async legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo already consumed by unified storage

Update passes the identical `objInfo` instance to Storage.Update and then, asynchronously, to Legacy.Update. The previous implementation computed the updated object once and passed legacy an updateWrapper around that fixed object; now Legacy.Update will call objInfo.UpdatedObject a second time, against the legacy store's old object and after the request has returned. UpdatedObjectInfo implementations are not guaranteed to be idempotent or safe to invoke twice (they may apply deltas, bump fields, or capture request-scoped state), so the legacy write can store different content than unified storage, or fail spuriously. Legacy should receive a wrapper carrying the already-computed/returned object, as before.

Async legacy failures are never logged

In all four async legacy goroutines the error is used only to set the metric's error flag (e.g. Create lines 55-56) and is otherwise discarded, with no log.Error via the request logger. Since mode 3 returns success to the client regardless, operators get no diagnosable record of which object failed to reach legacy storage or why; divergence will be discovered only via missing data. Log the error with the object name/kind inside each goroutine before recording the metric.

Async legacy writes use the request-scoped context and will usually be cancelled

Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection all launch the legacy write in a goroutine using `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where ctx is the incoming request context (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). The handler returns immediately after spawning the goroutine, at which point the apiserver cancels the request context, which cancels the derived timeout context. The legacy 'safety net' writes will therefore routinely fail with context-canceled before they run, silently diverging legacy storage from unified storage exactly as mode 3 is meant to prevent. The goroutine needs a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context preserving values) with its own timeout.

Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy writes and share one mock for both stores

The new Mode 3 tests construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock over a single shared testify mock.Mock, so a Storage call can be satisfied by an expectation registered for Legacy and vice versa (e.g. the TestMode3_Create 'storage fails' case at lines 37-44 registers only a Create expectation via setupLegacyFn yet the error surfaces from the Storage.Create call). The tests also return immediately without waiting for or asserting the background legacy goroutines (no AssertCalled/Eventually on Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection), so the defining behavior of mode 3 - the async legacy write - is untested, and stray goroutines can fire mock calls after the subtest ends, causing flaky cross-test interference under -race. Use separate mocks per store and synchronize/assert the legacy call in each test.

Storage failures in Create/Update are recorded as legacy durations

When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) for the time spent in storage, and Update does the same at line 129. No storage-duration sample is recorded and the legacy histogram is polluted with a failure/duration for an operation that never touched legacy storage. Dashboards/alerts on dual-writer latency and error rate per store will misattribute unified-storage failures to legacy. These should call recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

Two concurrent non-Dev callers can both observe a nil cache at line 41, then serialize on the write lock. The second caller does not recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock at line 48, so it reloads assets-manifest.json despite the first caller having populated the cache. More importantly, if that redundant reload fails, line 69 assigns its nil result over the valid cache and the caller returns an error instead of the already-available assets. Add a non-Dev cache recheck inside the write lock before reloading.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

Two concurrent non-Dev callers can both observe a nil cache at line 41, then serialize on the write lock. The second caller does not recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock at line 48, so it reloads assets-manifest.json despite the first caller having populated the cache. More importantly, if that redundant reload fails, line 69 assigns its nil result over the valid cache and the caller returns an error instead of the already-available assets. Add a non-Dev cache recheck inside the write lock before reloading.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the claimed data-race fix

The change introduces mutex protection for entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, ideally repeatedly under `go test -race` with both cache-miss and cache-hit paths. Without such a test, a future change that accesses the global outside entryPointAssetsCacheMu or mutates the shared returned value would not be caught by CI as a race regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions has inverted, dead logic

The helper computes enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false both when that value is true and in the fallthrough, so the flag and the branch are dead and the naming is inverted. This is misleading for a security-sensitive gate: a future editor following the variable name could easily re-enable the vulnerable path by 'fixing' the apparent inversion. Replace it with an explicit unconditional return false (with a comment referencing the removal), or remove the helper.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub DB breaks existing SQL tests with no updated/disabled tests

NewInMemoryDB's RunCommands and QueryFramesInto now always return 'not implemented', so the package-level TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/parser.go always errors and NewSQLCommand always rejects queries. The PR adds no test verifying SQL expressions are rejected, and does not update or skip the existing parser/SQL-command tests that expect DuckDB-backed table extraction and execution to succeed, leaving them failing against this stub. Update/skip those tests and add a regression test that a SQL expression is rejected regardless of the feature toggle.

false_positives.candidate:
Disabled-SQL check can panic on a nil FeatureToggles

enableSqlExpressions unconditionally calls h.features.IsEnabledGlobally even though it always returns false. If an ExpressionQueryReader is constructed without feature toggles (nil interface, e.g. in tests or other direct constructions), a SQL-type query now panics with a nil dereference instead of returning the intended 'not implemented' error. Since the result is unconditionally disabled, return false without dereferencing h.features.

Legacy SQL-command path bypasses the new SQL-expression gate

UnmarshalSQLCommand creates a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand without checking enableSqlExpressions or the sqlExpressions feature toggle, unlike the new check in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery. This legacy unmarshalling path therefore is not explicitly disabled; it currently fails only incidentally because sql.TablesList now delegates to the stub DB and errors. If the DuckDB-backed DB implementation is restored or replaced, this path would re-enable SQL expressions (the CVE-2024-9264 surface) without passing the gate. Gate or reject SQL in UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand as defense-in-depth.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized

BuildIndex now only holds cacheMu while inserting the finished index, and GetIndex uses a short RLock that returns nil while another goroutine is still building. Two concurrent getOrCreateIndex/Search/init calls for the same NamespacedResource can therefore both invoke BuildIndex, both call bleve.New/NewMemOnly (for file-backed indexes, both on the same directory path), both run the expensive builder, and then overwrite each other in b.cache. The losing bleve index is never closed, leaking file handles/directory locks, and concurrent file-backed creation can fail startup/search with index-lock/already-exists errors instead of sharing the one in-progress build as the old whole-build lock effectively did.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu.RLock. With BuildIndex now inserting into b.cache from many concurrent init workers and from lazy getOrCreateIndex builds, that unlocked iteration can race with a concurrent map write, which is a data race and can cause a fatal Go runtime 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic that crashes the process. TotalDocs should snapshot or iterate under RLock (taking care not to hold it while calling out if that can re-enter).

false_positives.candidate:
History and Origin panic when search is not configured

When opts.Search.Resources is nil (or the search backend is nil) NewResourceServer leaves s.search nil, yet History (line 925) and Origin (line 930) unconditionally dereference s.search, unlike Search which returns 'search index not configured'. After this PR removed the per-RPC Init guards, a History/Origin gRPC call to a server constructed without search will nil-pointer panic and crash the handler/process instead of returning an error.

NewResourceServer performs uncancellable init with the server's background context

NewResourceServer now synchronously calls s.Init(ctx) where ctx is the internally created context.Background()-derived watcher context (no caller context, deadline, or cancellation is accepted by the constructor). Building every search index can take arbitrarily long, and a caller that wants to abandon/shut down startup cannot cancel it and has no server handle yet on which to call Stop (which is the only place that cancels this ctx). Startup can thus hang indefinitely inside the constructor; previously a slow/failed init surfaced on the first RPC with that RPC's cancellable context.

init errgroup goroutines race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed

Inside searchSupport.init, each errgroup goroutine executes totalBatchesIndexed++ and assigns to the outer err variable captured from 'stats, err := ...' via '_, _, err = s.build(...)'. With SetLimit(initWorkers) running builds concurrently this is a data race: increments can be lost (wrong 'namespaced_indexed' span attribute) and per-namespace build errors can overwrite each other before 'return err', masking a failed namespace build or reporting another namespace's error. Use a local err per goroutine and an atomic/mutex-protected counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New test registers cleanup for a literal "alias" instead of the created IdPs

In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup is registered as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove rather than using each created alias ("idp-alias-" + i, and similarly "idp-alias-20" at line 425). This attempts to remove a provider literally named "alias" and does not clean up the 21 providers created by the test, leaving them in the shared test realm to potentially affect other tests in the class and masking failures from the cleanup call itself.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation can be skipped for IdPs linked to a disabled organization

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares getLoginPredicate() on the original and updated models, but the original model comes from getById() and is wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(), whose isEnabled() also returns false when the linked organization (or organizations for the realm) is disabled. The JPA delegate used by getForLogin() nevertheless included that IdP in the cached ID set based on its stored enabled flag. Therefore, while the organization is disabled, changing a login-relevant field such as hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or enabled to make the IdP ineligible makes both predicates evaluate to false (or otherwise appear unchanged), so no login-cache invalidation is registered. The stale ID remains cached and, once the organization is re-enabled, getForLogin() can return an IdP that the uncached JPA query would no longer return to callers that do not re-check those flags.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JCA provider

The CryptoProvider contract for getBouncyCastleProvider() is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type (typically SUN or SunJSSE). Callers that use the returned provider by name or for BouncyCastle-specific algorithms/services will fail or behave as if BouncyCastle were available when it is not. The Elytron provider already establishes the pattern of returning null when no BouncyCastle provider exists; returning an unrelated provider is more misleading and error-prone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is an extensible interface, but order() was added as an abstract method instead of a default method. Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against an earlier Keycloak version will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration calls order() during sorting, and source code for such implementations will no longer compile. Adding a default implementation (for example returning a neutral order) would preserve compatibility while allowing built-in providers to override it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
AuthzClient installs the stub crypto provider as a global first-wins singleton

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init(), and CryptoIntegration only initializes its static cryptoProvider once. When no higher-order provider is present this permanently installs AuthzClientCryptoProvider for the whole JVM, but that provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for PemUtils, CertificateUtils, signatures, ciphers, key factories, EC parameters, and most other CryptoProvider operations; a later attempt to initialize a full provider such as DefaultCryptoProvider will be ignored because the static provider is already set. Authz-client features or other Keycloak client code in the same process that need those operations will therefore fail unexpectedly.

ECDSA test uses one P-256 key for all curves and never verifies the converted signature

The test generates a single default EC key pair (P-256 on standard JDKs) and then uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512, and only asserts that DER-to-RS followed by RS-to-DER and back returns the same bytes. A self-consistent round trip can pass even if the DER output is not acceptable to a real verifier or if R/S padding/length handling for P-384 and P-521 is wrong. The test should generate a key pair on the curve matching each algorithm and verify that a signature converted to ASN.1 DER verifies with the JDK Signature object (and vice versa).

Equal-order providers are selected silently and nondeterministically

detectProvider() now sorts only by order() and silently ignores every provider after the first, replacing the previous fail-fast error for multiple providers. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order 200, so if more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order rather than configuration. In particular a non-FIPS provider could be selected where FIPS operation is required, silently weakening the intended security posture.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the all-clients pseudo-resource as a client id

resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) also returns the type resource whose name is literally 'Clients', created at schema initialization. If the caller is granted the scope on all clients, hasGrantedPermission succeeds for that resource and granted.add(resource.getName()) inserts 'Clients' into a set whose contract (Set<String> getClientsWithPermission) is client identifiers, while no actual client ids are added for clients that have no per-client resource yet. Callers filtering clients by id will miss those clients and may treat 'Clients' as an id.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NullPointerException when the Clients type resource does not exist

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code loads the Clients type resource and immediately passes it to findByResource(server, resource). getResourceTypeResource() can return null, for example in a realm created before the Clients type existed or if the type resource was not provisioned, so this dereference/query with a null resource can throw instead of simply denying the permission.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Existing FGAPv2 realms never receive the new Clients resource type or scopes

init() returns immediately whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore keep only the Users resource and the old scope set: the Clients all-resource resource and the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes are never created for them. Client permissions cannot be created or evaluated correctly in such upgraded realms until the admin-permissions client is recreated.

A negative value produces `num_processes <= 0`, an empty process-to-shards map, and therefore no flusher processes at all; submit() then finds no unhealthy processes to report while spans continue to be committed after being written to Redis but are never flushed. Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized

BuildIndex now only holds cacheMu while inserting the finished index, and GetIndex uses a short RLock that returns nil while another goroutine is still building. Two concurrent getOrCreateIndex/Search/init calls for the same NamespacedResource can therefore both invoke BuildIndex, both call bleve.New/NewMemOnly (for file-backed indexes, both on the same directory path), both run the expensive builder, and then overwrite each other in b.cache. The losing bleve index is never closed, leaking file handles/directory locks, and concurrent file-backed creation can fail startup/search with index-lock/already-exists errors instead of sharing the one in-progress build as the old whole-build lock effectively did.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

With BuildIndex now inserting into b.cache from many concurrent init workers and from lazy getOrCreateIndex builds, that unlocked iteration can race with a concurrent map write, which is a data race and can cause a fatal Go runtime 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic that crashes the process. Inside searchSupport.init, each errgroup goroutine executes totalBatchesIndexed++ and assigns to the outer err variable captured from 'stats, err := ...' via '_, _, err = s.build(...)'. With SetLimit(initWorkers) running builds concurrently this is a data race: increments can be lost (wrong 'namespaced_indexed' span attribute) and per-namespace build errors can overwrite each other before 'return err', masking a failed namespace build or reporting another namespace's error. Building every search index can take arbitrarily long, and a caller that wants to abandon/shut down startup cannot cancel it and has no server handle yet on which to call Stop (which is the only place that cancels this ctx). Startup can thus hang indefinitely inside the constructor; previously a slow/failed init surfaced on the first RPC with that RPC's cancellable context.

When opts.Search.Resources is nil (or the search backend is nil) NewResourceServer leaves s.search nil, yet History (line 925) and Origin (line 930) unconditionally dereference s.search, unlike Search which returns 'search index not configured'. After this PR removed the per-RPC Init guards, a History/Origin gRPC call to a server constructed without search will nil-pointer panic and crash the handler/process instead of returning an error.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so the new strategy provides no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() always enqueues and returns successfully, never raising MessageRejected. Despite the class docstring claiming natural backpressure, Arroyo will keep consuming from Kafka while workers fall behind, accumulating messages and WorkItem/result objects in memory indefinitely when one queue is slow or stuck, risking OOM instead of pausing consumption.

Closing a strategy permanently kills the shared queue pool that the factory reuses

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts down the queues and workers. That pool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() on every create_with_partitions() call (e.g. after a Kafka rebalance, when Arroyo closes the old strategy and creates a new one for the new assignment). Submits to the now-shutdown queues raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() catches at line 317 and then marks the offset complete, so messages for the new assignment can be committed without ever being processed. The factory only clears queue_pool in its own shutdown(), not when a strategy is closed.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() logs any exception from result_processor but unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() similarly marks offsets complete when decoding/grouping/enqueueing fails. The commit loop then treats those offsets as processed and commits them, contradicting the documented 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee: transient processing failures or poison messages are silently dropped and will not be redelivered.

Kafka offsets are committed from a background thread instead of the Arroyo processor thread

_commit_loop runs on its own thread and invokes commit_function, which in result_consumer.py calls Arroyo's Commit callable. Arroyo strategies are expected to invoke commit from the strategy's submit/poll/close calls on the StreamProcessor thread; calling it concurrently from this thread races StreamProcessor's own offset/assignment handling and can commit offsets against a stale or revoked assignment. Additionally, each strategy instance created for a rebalance spawns another commit thread over the same shared OffsetTracker, so two threads can race get_committable_offsets()/mark_committed() and double-commit.

close() stops the commit loop before draining queues, discarding commit progress

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown() to drain pending work. Workers then finish processing queued items and mark offsets complete, but no commit loop remains to commit those offsets and close() performs no final commit flush. On every graceful shutdown/rebalance, all work completed during the drain is therefore reprocessed on restart, causing duplicate result processing.

Offset scan is O(offset range) every second while a queue is blocked

get_committable_offsets() iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) for every partition on every 1-second commit loop iteration. The strategy's stated purpose is to survive a slow item blocking a queue; in exactly that case all later offsets accumulate in all_offsets/outstanding, so each poll rescans an ever-growing range (quadratic overall) and the sets grow without bound for as long as one offset is stuck, wasting CPU and memory.

OffsetTracker is never reset when partitions are revoked or reassigned

OffsetTracker keeps all_offsets, outstanding and last_committed forever, with no hook to clear a partition when Arroyo revokes it or when create_with_partitions is called with a new assignment. Stale outstanding offsets from a previous assignment block commits for a reassigned partition, and if offsets restart below the stale last_committed value (consumer-group reset, topic recreation, or reassignment with an earlier starting offset from the partitions mapping, which the strategy ignores), get_committable_offsets() can never advance past last_committed and commits silently stall.

false_positives.candidate:
Switching span buffers from sets to sorted sets breaks in-flight Redis data

The script and SpansBuffer now use ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZADD/ZSCAN on span-buf:s:* keys, but segments already buffered before deployment are Redis SETs created with SADD. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for sorted-set commands on those keys, so process_spans/flush_segments will error for in-flight segments until their TTL expires (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s), losing or stalling those spans. No migration, type check, or dual-read handling is included.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM and corrupts duplicate span scores

Both zunionstore calls omit an AGGREGATE clause, so Redis defaults to SUM. If the same span payload exists in both the destination and source sorted sets (e.g. a re-delivered span, or a span already zadded under the destination key by process_spans before the Lua merge), its score becomes the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values (roughly double, e.g. year 2077). Eviction via ZPOPMIN then orders by corrupted scores, so duplicated spans are effectively never evicted and eviction order no longer reflects end time. Use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) explicitly.

Unrelated audit-log pagination feature is bundled into the spans change

This PR is titled and described as a spans-buffer optimization, but it also adds a new user-controlled 'optimized_pagination' mode to the organization audit-log endpoint, gated on is_superuser/has_global_access and backed by the new OptimizedCursorPaginator. This changes behavior of a sensitive audit-log API (whose paginator is broken for datetime keys and crashes on negative offsets, per the paginator findings) without any endpoint tests, changelog, or feature-flag rollout. It should be split out and reviewed/tested independently rather than shipped hidden inside the spans change.

Redirect depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The redirect-following loop cap drops from 10000 to 1000 and the comment explaining that deeper segment trees may not be joined correctly is deleted. Traces whose parent chain exceeds 1000 redirects will now stop following redirects early, so spans land in separate span-buf:s:* sets and are flushed as fragmented/incomplete segments rather than one segment. This is a correctness regression for deep traces unrelated to the 1000-span eviction cap (chain depth and span count are different dimensions).

Flush-side max_segment_spans safeguard removed while insert cap is inconsistent

_load_segment_data no longer drops segments exceeding max_segment_spans (the metric and logger.error branch were removed), so the only remaining span-count protection is the Lua cap. That cap is hardcoded to 1000 while SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans defaults to 1001 and is configurable, and it only runs on the insert path: segments created before this change, created while script loading fails, or grown by the Python-side ZADD pipeline before Lua runs can now be loaded and flushed unbounded (bounded only by the 10MiB byte cap), reintroducing the memory/segment-size risk the removed guard protected against, with no metric when eviction truncates a segment.

process_batch now hard-requires end_timestamp_precise and will crash the batch if absent

Span previously did not need end_timestamp_precise; the existing consumer test payload omitted it and had to be modified in this PR to add it. Using val['end_timestamp_precise'] raises KeyError for any ingest-spans message lacking the field, failing the entire batch in process_batch (and, under Arroyo, causing redelivery/retry of the same poison batch) instead of defaulting the score (e.g. val.get('end_timestamp_precise', 0) or the message timestamp). Either tolerate a missing value or prove from the schema that it is mandatory and add a test for the missing-field case.

No test covers eviction, the sorted-set merge, or the reduced redirect depth

The test changes in this PR only add the new end_timestamp_precise argument to existing Span constructions. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify ZPOPMIN eviction (which spans survive, whether the root/segment span can be evicted, and final flushed contents), no test with duplicate payloads across merged sets to verify score handling, and no test near the new 1000 redirect-depth limit. The core behavioral change of the PR is therefore unverified.

The stale-folder denial can thus persist up to roughly a folder-cache TTL plus a denial TTL, so the fix does not reliably let creators reach resources in newly created folders.

However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without a content element

poll_feed unconditionally calls i.content.scrub for every item. Ordinary RSS items commonly have description instead of content (and Atom/RSS variants expose different fields), so i.content can be nil and this raises NoMethodError. Because the exception is inside rss.items.each with sidekiq retry disabled, one such item aborts the whole hourly poll and prevents all remaining items from being imported.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` unconditionally will cause a nil pointer exception (NoMethodError) because RSS feeds often lack a `content` element and instead use `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported feed/remote HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with cook_method raw_html, and Post#cook returns raw unchanged for such posts. Neither import nor absolutize_urls strips script tags, event-handler attributes, javascript: URLs, or other dangerous markup, and PollFeed passes RSS/Atom content directly into import. A malicious or compromised feed item can therefore store arbitrary HTML/JavaScript as post.cooked, which is rendered raw in Discourse and in embed views, giving stored XSS in forum visitors' browsers.

Concurrent imports for the same URL race the unique embed_url index

import does a non-atomic check-then-create: it looks up TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first and only creates the embed after PostCreator runs. Two concurrent RetrieveTopic/PollFeed executions for the same new URL can both see no embed, both create topics/posts, and then the second TopicEmbed.create! raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique from the unique index instead of returning the already-created post, failing the job after doing duplicate creation work. The lookup/create needs an atomic rescue/retry or locking strategy.

Embed controller spec expects synchronous TopicRetriever but controller enqueues a job

The 'tells the topic retriever to work' example stubs TopicRetriever.new/retrieve, but EmbedController#best never instantiates TopicRetriever; it calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...). The mock expectation will not be satisfied and this spec fails, leaving the actual enqueue arguments (user_id and embed_url) untested. The spec should expect Jobs.enqueue with :retrieve_topic instead.

Disqus import drops the category option and now depends on fetching the live source site

The import task removed the --category option and replaced local topic creation (with the thread's title, permalink body, created_at, and chosen category) with TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], ...), which performs open(url).read on each Disqus thread link. Existing invocations using -c will no longer place topics in the requested category, threads whose original site is offline, moved, or blocks fetching will fail the import, and the thread's original creation date is no longer used for the imported topic.

absolutize_urls only fixes root-relative URLs, leaving other relative links broken

absolutize_urls only rewrites href/src values that start with '/'. Feed and readability content frequently uses document-relative URLs such as href="page2.html" or src="images/pic.jpg" and protocol-relative URLs such as src="//cdn.example.com/x.jpg"; those are left untouched, so after import they resolve against the Discourse host instead of the source site and produce wrong links or 404 images in the imported post.

import_remote fetches arbitrary URLs server-side with no timeout or size limit

TopicEmbed.import_remote does open(url).read with no timeout, redirect restriction, or response-size cap before Readability parsing. Via EmbedController/RetrieveTopic the URL is user-influenced (constrained only by host equality at the retriever layer), so requests can make the server fetch large or slow resources on the embeddable host, exhausting job workers/memory; the fetched result is then published as a topic, which can also disclose content the server can reach but an anonymous visitor could not. Add timeouts, size limits, and scheme/host validation inside import_remote itself.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

false_positives.candidate:
Animated GIF detection fails for extensionless upload tempfiles

Upload and downloaded-file tempfiles normally have paths without a .gif extension. OptimizedImage.optimize selects its animated instructions only when the source path matches /\.GIF$/i, so passing tempfile.path here never selects that path despite allow_animation being supplied. The normal downsize instructions use `#{from}[0]`, selecting only the first frame, so an oversized animated GIF is silently flattened instead of being resized as an animation. The extensionless destination can also prevent ImageMagick from inferring the intended output format.

Failed image conversions are retried blindly and then ignored

The loop ignores the boolean result of OptimizedImage.downsize. If conversion fails—for example for an unsupported/corrupt image or an SVG matched by FileHelper.is_image?—it invokes the same failing conversion up to five times and then proceeds to Upload.create_for with the original oversized file. This wastes external-process work and makes the automatic-downsizing feature fail opaquely instead of falling back or reporting the conversion failure.

URL download limit is changed to a fixed 10 MB for every upload type

The API URL-download cap no longer uses SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb and is fixed at 10 megabytes regardless of whether the upload is an image or an attachment. This rejects remotely fetched files that the site configuration would allow above 10 MB, and it downloads non-image attachments up to 10 MB even when the applicable configured limit is lower; those attachments cannot be downsized and are only rejected after the transfer.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

TopicUser.find_by can return nil, for example when the user is receiving notifications through a watched category or has never visited/interacted with the topic in a way that created a topic_users row. Lines 107-113 then call tu.notification_level and tu.save! unconditionally, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing. false_positives.candidate: Per-topic unsubscribe mutates notification state on a GET request The new routes in config/routes.rb expose unsubscribe as GET and this action immediately changes and saves notification_level. Any logged-in browser request to the emailed URL therefore mutates state without confirmation or CSRF protection, so mail-scanner link prefetching, browser prefetch, or a cross-site /link to /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe can silently mute/downgrade a topic the user never intended to unsubscribe from. A state change like this should require POST (or an explicit confirmation step) with CSRF protection.

Unlike TopicsController#set_notifications, which uses TopicUser.change, this action assigns tu.notification_level and calls tu.save! directly. That bypasses the notifications_changed_at/notifications_reason_id (user_changed) bookkeeping and the MessageBus /topic/:id notification_level_change publish (and after-save observers) performed by TopicUser.change, so other open clients and topic-tracking state keep showing the old watching/tracking level until a full reload, and the change is not recorded as a user-initiated notification change.

config/locales/server.en.yml changes the shared unsubscribe_link string to include %{unsubscribe_url}, and both the HTML path here and body (line 90) render it via I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args) whenever add_unsubscribe_link is true. template_args only contains unsubscribe_url when the caller passes it, and MessageBuilder treats it as optional (only UserNotifications#send_notification_email supplies it). Any other current/future/test caller that sets add_unsubscribe_link: true without a topic-specific URL will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and fail to send; the new spec change that had to add unsubscribe_url to an existing generic builder illustrates the coupling. The per-topic line should be conditional or the translation should be given a safe default.

No tests cover the new unsubscribe endpoint or that the topic URL reaches the email

The only spec change adds unsubscribe_url to the fixture builder but adds no expectation that the unsubscribe_url appears in the body/HTML, and there are no controller specs for TopicsController#unsubscribe at all. The watching/tracking -> regular and regular/muted -> muted transitions, the missing-TopicUser case, the slug-redirect case, and unauthenticated/inaccessible-topic behavior are all untested, so the nil-row crash and level-transition regressions above would pass CI undetected.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Run from the repo root it reads/writes an .env outside the repository. This unrelated local-testing script will fail or touch the wrong file for Linux contributors.
